lessonLine: Grade 10 · Algebra II · Topic 3: Polynomial Functions · Lesson 3-4 — Dividing Polynomials
objectives: Identify quotients and remainders upon the division of polynomials.
Apply the Remainder Theorem and the Factor Theorem.
Use synthetic division to divide a polynomial by a linear polynomial with leading coefficient 1.
vocabList: Divisor ; factor ; Polynomial ; long division ; proper rational function ; Quotient ; Remainder ; synthetic division

outcome: Students will identify the quotient and the remainder when one polynomial is divided by another (objective 1; HSA.APR.D.6).
Students will apply the Remainder Theorem to find $p(a)$ as a remainder and the Factor Theorem to test a factor (objective 2; HSA.APR.B.2).
Students will use synthetic division to divide a polynomial by $x-a$, including a placeholder zero for a missing power (objective 3).
Three teaching days this week. If time runs short, cut Smart Production — never the Mastery Gate.
preclass: Pre-session home journey (already issued, with Lesson 3-3): watch “Remainder Theorem and Synthetic Division of Polynomials”, study two worked examples, answer three ungraded readiness questions. Submitted on the LMS before class.
Readiness questions: divide $x^{3}-3x^{2}+x-5$ by $x-2$; find $p(1)$ for a cubic; decide whether $x-2$ is a factor.
Evidence: the LMS answers feed the Diagnose.
diagTool: 3-question Quizizz (≤ 4 minutes) — the slide-4 checks: evaluate $p(x)=x^{3}-4x+2$ at $x=3$; factor $x^{2}-x-12$; list the coefficients of $2x^{3}-5x+1$ with the missing power.
diagGap: Expected gaps — Q1: $3^{3}$ evaluated as $9$. Q3: the zero for $x^{2}$ is left out.
Routing: 0–1 correct → re-teach substituting and the placeholder zero.  2 → straight to synthetic division.  3 → begin Investigate early.
instruction: Slide 5 — Long division (objective 1; HSA.APR.D.6). $x^{2}+5x+7=(x+2)(x+3)+1$, so the quotient is $x+3$ and the remainder is $1$; $\dfrac{2x^{3}-3x^{2}+4x-5}{x-1}=2x^{2}-x+3+\dfrac{-2}{x-1}$.

Slide 6 — Synthetic division (objective 3). $x^{3}+2x^{2}-4x+5$ by $x-1$ gives $x^{2}+3x-1$ remainder $4$; $x^{3}-4x^{2}+x+6$ by $x-2$ gives $x^{2}-2x-3$; $2x^{3}+x^{2}-13x+6$ by $x+3$ uses the box number $-3$.

Slide 7 — Remainder and Factor Theorems (objective 2; HSA.APR.B.2). $p(3)=5$ for $x^{3}-3x^{2}+x+2$; $x+1$ is a factor of $x^{3}+2x^{2}-x-2$, which factors as $(x+1)(x+2)(x-1)$; $k=-1$ makes $x-2$ a factor of $x^{3}+kx^{2}-4x+4$.

Slide 8 — Rewriting a rational expression (HSA.APR.D.6). $\dfrac{x^{2}+3x+5}{x+1}=x+2+\dfrac{3}{x+1}$ by inspection; $\dfrac{x^{3}+8}{x+2}=x^{2}-2x+4$, linking to the sum-of-cubes identity from Lesson 3-3.
Narration focus — for $x-a$ write $a$; a missing power needs a zero; the last number is the remainder.
quickCheck: On whiteboards, 60 seconds: divide $x^{3}+2x^{2}-5x+1$ by $x-1$ with synthetic division.
Expected: quotient $x^{2}+3x-2$, remainder $-1$. Watch for the box number $-1$ and for forgetting the remainder.
guided: Two identical “Give it a go” problems, worked with the teacher:
(1) Divide $x^{3}-2x^{2}-5x+6$ by $x-3$.  (2) Find the remainder when $x^{3}-5x+7$ is divided by $x-2$.
Worked live; students self-mark and circle their OWN first error.
independent: “Choose Your Route” sheet with live Pear Deck feedback. Routes name the task, not the student.

PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards: synthetic division, the Remainder Theorem and a factor test; then find the error in a box number. Done when: the box number has the opposite sign to the constant in the divisor and a zero remainder is linked to a factor.
APPLY — Use it in context. A box volume, a value of $k$, a rational expression and a value of $a$. Done when: the divisor is written as $x-a$ first and each answer is checked.
INVESTIGATE — Find out why. Prove $r=p(a)$, factor a cubic fully, and find remainders without dividing. Done when: the argument starts from $p(x)=(x-a)q(x)+r$.
Page 3: compare three division routes, judge three claims, test a What if...? idea. Every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
production: Non-routine transfer task — this context has not appeared in practice (slide 11).
A model Qiddiya water-slide tank has volume $V(x)=x^{3}+7x^{2}+14x+8$ m$^{3}$ and height $(x+2)$ m. The model values are invented for practice.
(a) Show that $x+2$ is a factor and find the base area. (b) Factor the base area and write $V(x)$ as three factors. (c) For $x=3$ find the volume from the factors and check it from $V(x)$.
Students then hand their reasoning to the AI challenger.
criteria: Minimum standard: the box number, the coefficients, the remainder read, the factors written, units (m, m$^{3}$).
Role of AI: challenger only — “Challenge my reasoning and point out any step I have not justified.” Never “solve this”.
Completed independently: the written justification for (a)–(c).
evidence: “Time to Check” — one individual task. No notes, no partner, no AI.
1. Divide $x^{3}+4x^{2}-x-6$ by $x+1$.  2. Is $x+2$ a factor of $x^{3}+x^{2}-4x-4$?  3. Find $k$ so that $x-2$ is a factor of $x^{3}+kx-6$.
Answers: 1. quotient $x^{2}+3x-4$, remainder $-2$.  2. $p(-2)=0$, so yes.  3. $8+2k-6=0$, so $k=-1$.
Done when: question 1 reads the remainder with its sign and question 2 states the Factor Theorem.
Scored live in Pear Deck and logged in the Impact Dashboard.
refinement: Students revise their tank reasoning using the AI challenger’s feedback and the teacher’s micro-conference note.

Final product (Canva one-pager, photographed solution, or 45-second voice note): the division, the Factor Theorem used, ONE non-example (box number $3$ for $x+3$), and why the three factors give the dimensions.
differentiation: PRACTICE — Secure the method. Six cards, a find-the-error line and a synthetic frame. Done when: the box number has the opposite sign.
APPLY — Use it in context. A box volume, a value of $k$, a rational expression and a value of $a$. Done when: each answer is checked.
INVESTIGATE — Find out why. Prove $r=p(a)$, factor a cubic and find remainders without dividing. Done when: the argument starts from $p(x)=(x-a)q(x)+r$.
No student is labelled; every student sits the same Mastery Gate.
saudi: Qiddiya water-slide tank and a model box; invented values.
exams: SAT — Advanced Math: when $p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}+kx-1$ is divided by $x-3$ the remainder is $5$, so $k=-1$. Trap: using $p(-3)$.
GAT (Qudurat) — the remainder of $x^{2}+1$ divided by $x-3$ against $10$: they are equal. Trap: assuming the divisor decides the size.
SAAT (Tahsili) — the quotient of $x^{3}-8$ divided by $x-2$ is $x^{2}+2x+4$. Trap: $x^{2}-2x+4$.
adaptive: Entry branch — the Quizizz result routes each student to the re-teach table, straight to the new content, or the Investigate prompt.
Mid-lesson branch — Pear Deck flags error patterns during independent practice; flagged students get a 2-minute micro-conference while others continue.
Exit branch — the Mastery Gate routes each student: PASS → Enrichment & Challenge; NOT YET → Targeted Learning Clinic at the start of the next lesson.
Routing is communicated privately through the LMS, never read aloud.
publication: Published to the class LMS portfolio; the strongest go on the Mathematics Department wall.

plan2026.tools: Quizizz (diagnostic) · Pear Deck (live practice feedback) · Whiteboards · Desmos (checking a remainder with p(a)) · Canva (final product) · Squared paper
plan2026.resources: Lesson presentation (15 slides) · “Choose Your Route” activity (3 pages) · Wayground kick-off
competencies: Dividing a polynomial by $x-a$ with synthetic division and reading the quotient and remainder.
Using $p(a)$ to find a remainder and to test a factor.
technology: Quizizz live diagnostic with instant gap analysis.
Desmos: check that a zero of $p$ gives a zero remainder.
reallife: A tank volume that factors into length, width and height.
Missing values in a model so that a division comes out exactly.
values: Accuracy — the box number and every sign are written before they are used.
soft: Explaining in words why a zero remainder means a factor.
phases: FIKR Phase 1 — Diagnose. 3-question Quizizz: evaluating a polynomial, factoring, listing coefficients. Results read as a gap map and used to route students.
FIKR Phase 2 — Targeted Instruction. Long division; synthetic division; the Remainder and Factor Theorems; rewriting a rational expression.
FIKR Phase 3 — Practice. Two identical “Give it a go” problems; then students choose a route and may switch. Compare routes and judge the claim. Pear Deck feedback.
FIKR Phase 4 — Production. Qiddiya water-slide tank; AI as challenger only.
FIKR Phase 5 — Proof of Learning. “Time to Check”. No notes, no partner, no AI.
FIKR Phase 6 — Smart Production. Make a cubic with a chosen factor, divide, swap and test; publish to the LMS portfolio.
assessment: Diagnostic quiz — gap map, not a grade.
Whiteboard check (80% threshold) and “Give it a go” — self-marked.
Project task sheet against its “Done when…” criteria.
“Time to Check” — Mastery Gate, scored live.
Final product graded on reasoning and clarity.
plan2026.closure: Two minutes of peer show-and-tell, then: “Which is harder — choosing the box number, or remembering the placeholder zero?”
plan2026.homework: Upload the final product to the LMS portfolio. Pear Deck practice set (12 questions, choose your route). Schoology homework quiz for Lesson 3-4. Clinic group: bring your Time to Check paper.

classwork.subtitle: Show all your working. Read the vertex with the signs flipped, divide 4p by 4, and measure to the focus and the directrix. A correct answer with no working is only half an answer.

sections.h: Part A — Focus, directrix and the equation
text: 1.  A parabola has focus $(0,2)$ and directrix $y=-2$. For the point $P(4,2)$, find $PF$ and $PD$. Is $P$ on the parabola? Then derive the equation using $PF=PD$.
2.  Derive the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,5)$ and directrix $y=-5$. State $p$.
3.  Write the equation of the parabola with focus $(0,-4)$ and directrix $y=4$. Which way does it open?

sections.h: Part B — Reading the equation and the graph
text: 4.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus, the directrix and the axis of symmetry.
5.  Find the vertex, $p$, the focus and the directrix. Which way does it open?
6.  The graph shows a parabola. Its vertex and focus are marked. Read them, then write the equation in standard form and the directrix.

sections.h: Part C — Graphing from key features
text: 7.  Graph $(x-1)^{2}=8\,(y+1)$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
8.  Graph $y^{2}=-8x$ on the grid. Mark the vertex, the focus and the directrix, and the two points at the height of the focus.
9.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
10.  Complete the square and find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.
11.  Divide first, then complete the square. Find the vertex, the focus and the directrix.

sections.h: Part E — In context and in your own words
text: 12.  A model fountain jet on the Jeddah waterfront has its apex at $(0,8)$ and lands at $(\pm12,\,0)$ (metres, model values). Write its equation and find the focus. How high is the jet at $x=6$?
13.  A model satellite dish is $1.8$ m wide and $0.27$ m deep. Put the vertex at the origin, find $4p$ and say how far the receiver sits from the vertex.
14.  Show that the width of $x^{2}=4py$ at the height of the focus is $4\lvert p\rvert$. Use it to find the two points of $x^{2}=20y$ at that height.

pbl.title: Jeddah Satellite Dish Installer
pbl.subtitle: A 20-minute group project. Work in fours. Every member signs the sheet.
pbl.driving: A Jeddah installer has four dishes and one receiver arm that is 1.1 m long. Which dishes can hold the receiver exactly at the focus, and what does the shape of the dish tell you?
situation: A classroom model (invented for practice, not real figures): each dish is a parabola with its vertex at the origin, opening upward. Its width and depth are in the table. The receiver must sit at the focus, a distance $p$ above the vertex.

For each dish the group finds $4p$ from the rim point, writes the equation, finds $p$, and says whether a $1.1$ m arm is long enough. Then the group explains how the depth of a dish changes its focal length.
steps: For each dish, write the rim point $(x_{1},y_{1})$: half the width across, the full depth up. Write $x^{2}=4py$ with the rim point substituted.
Find $4p$ and $p$ for every dish and write each equation. Fill the table.
Which dishes can hold the receiver at the focus with a $1.1$ m arm? Check one dish: the rim point is equally far from the focus and the directrix.
What happens to $p$ as the dishes get deeper for their width? Which dish is the most tightly curved?
One sentence for the installer: how can you tell where the receiver goes from the width and depth alone?

standards: Know and apply the Remainder Theorem: For a polynomial p(x) and a number a, the remainder on division by x - a is p(a), so p(a) = 0 if and only if (x - a) is a factor of p(x).

Rewrite simple rational expressions in different forms; write a(x)/b(x) in the form q(x) + r(x)/b(x), where a(x), b(x), q(x), and r(x) are polynomials with the degree of r(x) less than the degree of b(x), using inspection, long division, or, for the more complicated examples, a computer algebra system.
Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it.
